analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps to $15 an hour, then indexes it to inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in House committees after being introduced by one representative and three cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $8 an hour almost immediately, then by $1 each year until it reached $15 seven years later. After that, the Department of Labor would raise it automatically each year with the cost of living. Employers whose lowest-paid workers earn at least $1 above the minimum would get a small tax credit to offset the increase. The bill was referred to two House committees, sent to a subcommittee, and never advanced further before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid near the federal minimum wage, most of whom work in retail, food service, and other hourly jobs. The bill would have raised their pay in scheduled steps to $15 an hour, then kept it rising with inflation so it would not erode again [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers paid near the minimum wage

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $8 an hour within roughly a month of enactment, then by $1 a year until it reaches $15 seven years later [S2][S3].

After reaching $15, the minimum wage would rise automatically each year with increases in the Consumer Price Index, preventing the eroding value that left the federal minimum unchanged from 2009 [S2][S3].

Gives employers whose lowest-paid worker earns at least $1 above the federal minimum a tax credit equal to 6.2% of wages paid to hourly workers earning up to $15, softening the cost of the increase for employers who already pay more [S2][S3].
Requires the Labor Department to publish each scheduled increase 60 days in advance in the Federal Register and online, so businesses and workers know what is coming [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with low-wage workforces, who would pay higher hourly wages over seven years. The tax credit would offset some of that cost for employers already paying above the minimum. Consumers could see some of the higher labor costs passed through in prices [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Phasing in a federal $15 minimum wage over seven years would raise labor costs substantially for businesses in low-wage regions and industries; some employers might respond by cutting hours, slowing hiring, automating, or raising prices, because the federal minimum covers areas where living costs and prevailing wages are far lower than in big cities [S2][S3].
A single national wage floor ignores large regional differences in prices and existing wages, which is why most minimum-wage increases in recent years have been set at the state or city level [S2].

The bill's employer tax credit reduces federal revenue; the bill pairs a mandate on employers with a tax break for them, and the credit only helps employers already paying above the minimum, not those the wage floor hits hardest [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and certain for the workers covered: a scheduled path to $15 an hour with inflation protection. The costs fall on employers and, in part, on consumers, and the size of any job losses from a national $15 floor is genuinely contested among economists. The bill tried to manage this with a slow seven-year phase-in and a tax credit for higher-paying employers, but a single national number still fits some regional economies better than others. It was a real, targeted improvement for low-wage workers with acknowledged and debated costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Norcross introduced the Fair Wage Act on February 9, 2016, with Reps. Pallone and Watson Coleman as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced [S1][S5].
On March 23, 2016, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections within the Education and the Workforce Committee — the last action ever taken on it [S5].
No further action was recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have paid the higher wages — particularly in retail, restaurants, and other low-wage industries — are better off because the bill never advanced; minimum-wage workers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Donald Norcross
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship; no committee ever acted on it.

for.name: Reps. Frank Pallone and Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.role: Original cosponsors, U.S. House of Representatives
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the bill attracted three cosponsors total and no further support in the record.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and sent it to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections; never held a hearing or markup, and the bill died there.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for the bill's tax-credit provision; took no recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by three New Jersey Democrats with three Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support in the record, and it died in the Republican-controlled House without a hearing or vote.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (retail, restaurants, hospitality, and other hourly-work industries)
industries.note: If enacted, the bill would have raised their labor costs by requiring wages to climb to $15 an hour over seven years, with a partial tax credit for employers already paying above the minimum. Because the bill died, these costs never materialized.

The bill would have created a new employment-tax credit, adding administrative work and a new credit for employers, but this is a minor mechanical effect rather than a substantive interest in the bill.
